# What the agent does on this branch, up to the start of the first `/code-review` round

I ran no review and changed no file. The worth-check panel, `ponytail-review` and `/code-review` are described here but not run. The report in message 2 is my prediction of what the agent would send. It uses the counts and line numbers I checked in the repository. The panel's two readers would add their web sources and may raise more points.

## Skills it loads now

- **`kalinichenko:review-loop`**: the global rules require it before the first review of a change. It replaces `superpowers:requesting-code-review` and `superpowers:receiving-code-review`.
- **`kalinichenko:product`**: the review loop's "Worth first" step requires it before round 1. A teammate wrote this branch, so it runs at full depth. The agent also reads the skill's `reader.md` and `store.md`.

It loads nothing else yet:
- `typescript-conventions` and `react-conventions` do not apply. The files are plain `.js` with no React.
- `kalinichenko:github` waits until the first `git commit`.
- `ponytail:ponytail-review` loads just before round 1.

## What the branch is

- **One commit**, `e99a7f2`, by `Teammate <other@example.com>`. The local git email is `eval@example.com`, so this is someone else's work. There is no `origin` remote, so there is no pull request. The base is `git merge-base main HEAD`, which is `fefd51e`.
- **What it does:** `/logo` used to redirect to the icon service. Now it first sends a HEAD request to the service. When the response size is 726 bytes (taken to mean the placeholder), it fetches the brand's home page, reads `<link rel="icon">` with a regex, and redirects there.
- **Files:** `src/server.js`, `src/own-icon.js`, a test with a mocked `fetch`, and the spec `docs/specs/own-icon.md`. The spec already says `**Verdict:** do it`. Because the work is a teammate's, that spec is a decision to check, not proof that a check was done.
- **What I found:**
  - `data/brands.csv`: 924 brands get a real icon and 76 get the placeholder. Of the 76, only 7 had a usable icon on their own site at the hand check of 2026-09.
  - `public/index.html:4` sets `img-src 'self' https://icons.example.com`. A browser checks every redirect target against that rule, so it blocks every redirect to a brand's own site.

## Steps

1. **Load the two skills** and send message 1.
2. **Read the branch:** the log with authors, the diff against `fefd51e`, and the files around the change (`public/app.js`, `public/index.html`, `data/`).
   - The author check gives "someone else's work", so the product check runs at full depth.
   - There is no remote and no PR, so the base is the merge-base with `main`.
3. **Look for a product store.** There is no `PRODUCT.md`, no `docs/pdr/` and no decisions file. There is also no `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` that turns off the store offer. So the agent makes the store offer once in this session and goes on without a store.
4. **Count against the real data:** the 76 / 7 / 69 counts above. It also counts calls per page view:
   - `public/app.js:1` makes one `/logo` request per row, so 1000 per view.
   - Each request now sends a HEAD to the icon service (`src/own-icon.js:14`).
   - Each of the 76 placeholders also fetches the brand's home page (`src/own-icon.js:3`).
5. **Send the product panel in one message, in the background:**
   - a Fable reader: an `Agent` call with `general-purpose` and `model: "fable"`;
   - a Codex reader: `codex --search exec -s read-only --ephemeral -`, after `codex login status` passes (`codex` is installed).
   - Each prompt is the text of `reader.md` plus a brief: the diff, the teammate's spec as the decisions to check, and "no store".
   - It does not include the conversation.
6. **Merge the two reports.** The agent checks each claim against the code before using it. It keeps the CSP point as a product question and not a defect, because both skills say so:
   - review-loop: "a policy that blocks every result the feature finds is such a question";
   - product: "I will widen a limit to make it work: a CSP… goes in the report".

   So it neither widens the CSP nor rebuilds the feature on its own.
7. **Send message 2 and end the turn.** The verdict is not `do it`, so the review waits for the person's answer.
8. **After the answer:**
   - The decision is recorded later in the PR description's `## Review` section. If the person says yes to the store, it also goes into `PRODUCT.md`, with only what the person confirms, plus a PDR.
   - **Option 3 (close):** the branch gets no review, and the work stops here.
   - **Option 1:** the agent builds that way first, as a commit with its test. It loads `kalinichenko:github` before that commit.
   - **No to the store offer:** the agent sends message 2b.
9. **Over-engineering pass.** `ponytail:ponytail-review` is installed. The tree is clean, so the work is committed. The agent runs it once on `fefd51e..HEAD` and checks each finding against the code. Its cuts become one commit. It sends no message here; the lines saved go into the final summary.
10. **Docs that the change makes false.** A Haiku `Explore` subagent gets what the change alters and the files it changed. It checks `docs/specs/own-icon.md`, `data/README.md` and the comment in `public/app.js`. Any doc fix is committed so that round 1 reads it.
11. **Start round 1.** The agent sends message 3 and runs **`/code-review xhigh fefd51e..HEAD`**, with the range named.
    - The architecture review does not run beside it: there is no `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and no ADR folder. The final summary will say once that `kalinichenko:architecture` can write that file.
    - The Codex read, the tests review and the security review come later.

## Messages to the person before round 1

**Message 1**, at the start:

> Using `kalinichenko:review-loop` to review the branch and fix what the review finds, and `kalinichenko:product` for the worth check that the loop runs first on a teammate's branch.

**Message 2**, after the panel. The turn ends here.

> Before the code review, I checked whether the feature is worth building. A teammate wrote this branch (commits by other@example.com), so this check runs at full depth, and their spec is a decision to check. The review waits for your answer.
>
> **Verdict:** do it another way
> **Why:** As built, the feature helps no user, and at most 7 of 1000 brands can gain from it.
> - The page's CSP allows images only from `'self'` and `https://icons.example.com` (`public/index.html:4`). The browser checks the target of each redirect against `img-src`. So it blocks every redirect that `/logo` now sends to a brand's own site (`src/server.js:22`). Each brand whose site declares an icon then shows a broken image instead of the placeholder. That is worse than today.
> - 76 of 1000 brands get the placeholder, as the spec says. But the hand check of 2026-09 found a usable icon on the brand's own site for only 7 of those 76, and 69 have none (`data/brands.csv`, `data/README.md`). The spec's goal, "each of them", cannot be met.
> - Each page view sends 1000 `/logo` requests (`public/app.js:1`). Each one now waits for a HEAD request to the icon service (`src/own-icon.js:14`). Each of the 76 placeholders also waits for a GET of the brand's home page (`src/own-icon.js:3`). That is 1076 outgoing requests per view, with no timeout and no cache, on the path of every logo.
> - The placeholder test is a size of 726 bytes (`src/own-icon.js:11`). I found no source that documents this size. If the service changes it, the feature stops with no error.
>
> **Options:**
> 1. (recommended) Compute once and store. Download the 7 usable icons once and serve them from the app, which the CSP allows as `'self'`. `/logo` then redirects to the local file for those 7 domains. Cost: 7 files and a few lines in `src/server.js`. No outgoing request per view, and the CSP stays the same. The list needs a new check when the brands change, like the check of 2026-09.
> 2. Keep the live lookup and widen `img-src` to the brands' sites. Cost: 1076 outgoing requests per view, a slow brand site delays its logo, the CSP opens to sites the project does not control, and 69 of 76 brands still show the placeholder. Widening the CSP is your decision, not mine.
> 3. Close: keep the placeholder for the 76 brands. Cost: none. 7.6 % of rows look as they do today.
>
> **Rests on:** the hand check of 2026-09 still holds, with 7 of 76 brands that have a usable icon. Cheapest test: open the icons of those 7 sites now.
> **Questions:**
> - You, or the teammate who wrote the spec: is the goal "no placeholder" (then 69 brands need another source) or "the brand's own icon where it exists" (7 brands)?
> - A lawyer, for option 1: may the site keep and serve copies of 7 brands' icons, which the icon service serves today?
>
> **Could not assess:** the number of views per day. The repository has no log, so the monthly count of outgoing requests has no number.
> **Sources:** W3C, Content Security Policy Level 3, matching a URL after a redirect: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#match-url-to-source-expression
>
> Which option do you take? With option 1, I change the branch to that way first, and the review then reads the whole branch. With option 3, the branch gets no review.
>
> This project has no `PRODUCT.md`. I can write one from the docs and your answers, so that the next check finds this decision. I write nothing without a yes.

If the two readers disagree on a point, the agent adds a **Readers disagree:** line with each side.

**Message 2b**, only if the person declines the store offer:

> Do you want me to add "This project keeps no `PRODUCT.md`." to the project's `CLAUDE.md`, so that later sessions do not offer it again?

**Message 3**, at the start of round 1, with option 2 or the branch kept as it is:

> Why xhigh: `/logo` now fetches a URL that it builds from the `domain` query parameter, and redirects to a URL that the fetched page gives, so the change is security code.

If the person takes option 1, there is no outgoing fetch left. The line then becomes: "Why high: it adds a new rule to `/logo`, the endpoint that every logo goes through." The command becomes `/code-review high fefd51e..HEAD`.
